title: Heat and temperature (part 3)
textbookText: temperature of a system is the property which finally acquires the same value as all other bodies placed in the thermal contact. The body which loses heat in thermal contact is said to be at higher temperature whereas the body which gains heat is said to be at lower temperature. The body which gains heat goes on warming up and its temperature increases due to added heat energy. Hence temperature is the effect of heat. A body at higher temperature gives more severe pain of hotness even if it may have low amount of heat. But a body at low temperature gives less severe pain of hotness even if it may have high amount of heat. In molecular concept, temperature of a body gives the measure of average kinetic energy of its molecules. It is not defined for single particle but for a system of large number of particles. Hence temperature is macroscopic parameter. The unit of temperature is Kelvin (K) in SI system and other commonly used units are degree Celsius (C) and degree Fahrenheit (F). 9.5 Effects of Heat When heat is applied to a body, it may bring the following changes: 1. Thermoelectric effect: If a temperature difference is maintained between two junctions of a closed loop made from a pair of dissimilar metal wires, an emf is developed. This emf produces electric current in the circuit. This effect of heat is called thermoelectric effect. 2. Generation of light energy: When we increase the temperature of a substance sufficiently high, the substance starts emitting light. 3. Change in electrical resistance: On increasing the temperature, electrical resistance of a conductor increases but in case of semiconductor electrical resistance decreases. 4. Change in physical properties: Change in temperature, volume, state, colour, viscosity, elasticity, solubility rate, rate of chemical reaction and surface tension, etc. are the physical changes carried out by the application of heat. 5. Change in chemical properties: Ignition of paper, boiling of egg, etc. are the examples of chemical changes carried out by the application of heat. Sample Questions: 1. Can an object be hotter than another if they are at the same temperature? Explain. 2. What is the temperature of a vacuum? 3. Why does heat flow from a body at higher temperature to a body at lower temperature? 4. Which factor determines the flow of heat between two bodies in thermal contact? 9.6 Thermal Equilibrium Fig. 9.3: Thermal Equilibrium Physics, Grade 11 | 211

When a cup of hot tea is put on the table and after a short period of time, the temperature of the tea will also be same as that of the surroundings. This is because when two bodies at different temperatures are brought in thermal contact, heat flows from a body at higher temperature to a body at lower temperature. So, temperature of hot body goes on decreasing and temperature of cold body goes on increasing until both acquire equal value of temperature. After attaining equal temperature net flow of heat between those bodies becomes zero, and they are said to be thermal equilibrium. Actually, exchange of heat between two bodies in thermal contact does not stop at thermal equilibrium, but it occurs at same rate in opposite direction. Using this idea of thermal equilibrium temperature readings are taken otherwise a thermometer is worthless because it always registers the temperature of its own thermometric substance.

“Two bodies are said to be in thermal equilibrium if there is no net flow of heat between them even if they are in thermal contact”. In other words, two physical systems are in thermal equilibrium if there is no net flow of thermal energy between them when they are in thermal contact. Principle of thermal equilibrium is used to measure the temperature of a body from a thermometer. 9.7 Thermal Equilibrium as a Working Principle of Mercury Thermometer To measure the temperature of a body, the bulb of the thermometer and the object whose temperature is to be measured are brought into thermal contact, and sufficient time is allowed for them to reach thermal equilibrium. At thermal equilibrium, both the thermometric substance and the object attain the same temperature. However, the temperature reading is solely indicated by the thermometer, representing the temperature of its thermometric substance. Therefore, the reading displayed by the thermometer is the temperature of its own thermometric substance. By employing the concept of thermal equilibrium, we can infer that this temperature is also the temperature of the given object. Thus, the principle of thermal equilibrium is employed in measuring the temperature of a body using a thermometer. 9.8 Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics Statement:“When two bodies A and B are in thermal equilibrium separately with a third body C then, first two bodies A and B themselves must be in thermal equilibrium”.
